To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the conclusions drawn by data miners about the best way to improve effort estimates and defect predictions are unstable.
(1) global models tend to be better than local models for effort estimation but worse for defect prediction and (2) local models are better for defect prediction when the data is not too skewed.
the conclusions of effort estimation and defect detection studies are unstable and that the instability is due to the use of local models, i.e. models built on data from only one project or module.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: * What are the most important factors that influence the effectiveness of effort estimation and defect predictions?
how to best combine global and local models for effort estimation or defect prediction, so that we can improve our estimates and predictions.
how to improve the accuracy of software effort estimation and defect predictions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most effective action is to improve the local model.
the best local models for effort and defect prediction are not necessarily the best for the whole set of projects or software modules.
the most effective action depends on the specific project and module.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
local models are more accurate than global models.
the most effective action is to improve the model, not to improve the data.
the best local rule is often different than the best global rule, and that local rules are better than global rules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the best action depends on whether one is trying to improve effort estimation or defect prediction.
the instability of local and global conclusions may be caused by the instability of the data mining models themselves.
this instability is due to the fact that different projects or modules exhibit different characteristics.
